title: Saving your prompts and reusing them every day
promise: You'll come out of this with a Project set up in ChatGPT and another in Claude, your instructions inside, and a file with five of your own prompts ready to paste and fill in in thirty seconds.
why: Marta sells climbing gear in Vitoria and has 300 products with no listing written. The first Monday it took her forty minutes to get ChatGPT to write a listing in the tone she wanted, and it came out perfect. The second Monday she couldn't find that conversation among the forty she had, rewrote it from memory, and it came out worse. Six Mondays running, she's been paying the same forty-minute toll for a job she'd already solved once: what she's missing isn't knowing how to write prompts, it's a place to save them.

theory.title: The problem isn't writing the prompt. It's finding it again
theory.text: A good prompt almost never comes out on the first try. It comes out on the fourth attempt, after you've told the AI three times: no, not like that, shorter, no exclamation points. That fourth attempt is the one worth money, and it's exactly the one that ends up buried in the middle of a thirty-message conversation you won't even remember having in two weeks. Chat history looks like an archive, but it isn't: it sorts your conversations by date, not by what they were for, and the search only finds words you remember having typed. What happens then is you rewrite the prompt from memory, and the memory version is always the first attempt, not the fourth. Saving prompts isn't a habit for tidy people: it's the difference between the AI saving you time once versus saving you time every week. The doubt that'll come up is "isn't it faster to just rewrite it?" The first time, yes; by the sixth, you've already lost four hours.
theory.analogy: It's the difference between cooking from memory and having the recipe written down. The first time the stew came out perfect, you remembered everything. By the sixth stew you no longer know if it was two tablespoons of paprika or three, and it comes out different every time.
theory.example: Marta searches "product listing" in her ChatGPT history and gets eleven conversations. She opens four before finding the right one, because the title ChatGPT gave that conversation was "Harness description." Twelve minutes spent hunting for a text she'd already written.

theory.title: A reusable prompt has a fixed part and some blanks
theory.text: A one-off message works for today. A template works forever, and the difference between the two is tiny: separating what repeats from what changes. Everything that stays the same next Monday you write out as-is: who the AI is, what job it does, what tone it writes in, what format you want, the maximum word count, what it must never do. Everything that changes each time you turn into a blank, written in capital letters and brackets, with a name that's self-explanatory: [PRODUCT NAME], not [X]. Capitalizing the blank isn't a whim: when you paste the prompt into the text box, whatever's in capitals jumps out at you and you know exactly what's left to fill in before hitting send. And if you forget to fill one in, the AI will tell you instead of making something up, because a bracket with capitals inside doesn't look like real data. A good saved prompt has between two and five blanks: if it has twelve, you've saved a form, and filling it in will tire you out more than writing the request from scratch.
theory.analogy: A lease agreement. The body of the lease hasn't changed in twenty years. The only things filled in by hand each time are the name, the unit, the date, and the amount. Nobody drafts the whole lease from scratch for every new tenant.
theory.example: Marta's template starts fixed: "You're the copywriter for a climbing gear shop in Vitoria. You write product listings in plain casual English, exactly 90 words, no emojis, and never using the word experience." And it continues with the blanks: [PRODUCT NAME], [PRICE], [THREE TECHNICAL SPECS FROM THE LABEL], [WHAT TYPE OF CLIMBING IT'S FOR]. Four blanks, forty seconds to fill in.

theory.title: The three drawers: global, project-level, and loose
theory.text: There are three places an instruction can live, and putting it in the wrong one is what turns this into a mess. The global drawer is your account's custom instructions: they apply to absolutely everything you do with that AI, so only put things there that are always true, like "talk to me in plain, casual English, and if you use a technical term, translate it in parentheses." The project drawer is a specific Project's instructions: they apply only inside that box, and that's where everything true only for that job goes, like your shop's tone, your products, your customers, your style pet peeves. The loose drawer is your prompt file: that's where the specific requests you repeat live, the ones with blanks that you paste into the text box when you need them. The rule is simple: if it applies to everything you do, it goes global; if it applies to one job, it goes in the project; if it's a task you repeat, it goes in your file. And if you write the same thing in all three, nothing bad happens, except that one day you'll change one and not the others, and then the AI gets two contradicting orders. When that happens, the instruction closest to the message almost always wins: what you write in the text box outweighs the project's instructions, and those outweigh the global ones.
theory.example: Marta put "always answer in under 100 words" in her global instructions and then spent two weeks fighting the AI cutting off the long emails she needed for customers. That rule wasn't global, it belonged to her product-listing project. She moved it to the right drawer and the problem was gone.

theory.title: ChatGPT Projects from the inside
theory.text: A ChatGPT Project is a folder with three things inside: a name, an instructions text, and some files. Everything you say inside that folder arrives already carrying the instructions and with the files available, without you having to paste anything. The files are the most underrated part: if you upload your price list as a PDF, your catalog as an Excel, and a document with five of your old texts, the AI stops making up your data and your tone, because it has them right there. How many files you can upload depends on your plan, and right now it's five on the free account, twenty-five on Plus, and forty on Pro; check it on your screen, because these numbers change. Conversations you open inside the project stay inside the project, which also fixes the problem of finding them: instead of a jumbled forty-chat history, you have one folder for the shop and another for your website. Serious warning: if you delete a project, every conversation inside it gets deleted too, and there's no recycle bin to recover them from. And the question nagging you: no, this isn't the same as ChatGPT's memory. Memory picks up loose bits from all your conversations on its own and you don't have tight control over what it saves; the project is a box you fill yourself and know exactly what's inside.
theory.analogy: Memory is a junk drawer where someone keeps tossing papers on your behalf. The project is a labeled folder you filled yourself and know the contents of by heart.
theory.example: Marta's project is called "Climbing shop listings." Instructions: 180 words with her tone and her banned words. Files: the Excel catalog with the 300 products, the 2026 pricing PDF, and a document with six old listings she liked. Now she types "listing for the Petzl Corax" and gets it right the first time.

theory.title: Claude: instructions, projects, and styles, and what each one costs
theory.text: Claude splits this into two, and understanding it saves you money. On one side are your personal preferences, which live in Settings inside your profile and are free: a text box where you write how you always want it to talk to you, and it works the same on the free account as on paid. On the other side are Claude Projects, which carry their own instructions and their own knowledge base (the files you upload), and those do require a paid plan: Claude Pro runs about $20/month, or about $17/month if you pay for the whole year up front. And there's a third thing that's Claude-only and almost nobody uses: Styles, which are also free and control how the answer sounds, not what it says. You can create a style by pasting three texts you wrote and saying "always write like this," and from then on you pick it with a button next to the text box. The mental split is this: instructions say what it does and doesn't do, style says how it sounds. If you don't want to pay yet, don't: with personal preferences and your own style you get most of the benefit for zero dollars, and you keep long prompts in your file and paste them by hand. Before entering a card anywhere, check the price on the payment screen, since these figures change several times a year.
theory.example: Marta only uses Claude for tricky supplier emails and doesn't pay for Claude Pro. She has her personal preferences filled in ("plain casual English, don't recap what I just said before answering, three paragraphs max") and a style called "Marta emails" built from four of her 2025 emails. Zero dollars a month.

theory.title: The library: one file, six fields, and the three-times rule
theory.text: Your prompt library needs to be a single file, and it doesn't matter whether it's a Google Doc, a phone note, or a Word file on your desktop: what kills it is having it scattered across four places. Each saved prompt needs six fields, no more: the name, when I use it, the blanks that need filling, the full prompt, how I know it turned out well, and the version with the date. The field that'll surprise you most is "how I know it turned out well," because it forces you to write two checkable signals (for example: it has 90 words and the word experience doesn't appear), and that's what lets you judge an answer in five seconds instead of reading the whole thing and still being unsure. The name always starts with a verb, because you don't search for "listings," you search for "write product listing." The rule for deciding what to save is the three-times rule: the first time you ask for something, you just write it; the second time you tough it out; the third time you save it. And you need to retire things: when a prompt fails you twice in a row, don't patch it with an extra message in the chat, fix it in the file and bump the version to v2 with today's date. Every time a new model comes out, take your top five prompts and retest them for an afternoon: sometimes a long prompt full of warnings stops being necessary because the new model no longer makes that mistake, and you've been dragging around useless paragraphs for half a year.
theory.example: Marta's library fits in a two-page Google Doc with seven entries. The first is called "Write product listing," it's on v3 dated 03/12/2026, and in the field for how she knows it turned out well it says two lines: 90 words counted, and it mentions the label's actual measurement, not a made-up one.

tasks.title: Write down what you ask the AI every week
tasks.where: In a phone note or on paper, no AI open yet
tasks.action: Write a list of things you've asked an AI for more than once in the last month. Don't stop to word them nicely: five lines of three words each is fine. Think boring and repeated, not brilliant: answering customer emails, summarizing meetings, writing copy for your website, pulling tasks out of meeting minutes, translating messages. If you get more than eight, cross out until you're down to five: those are what you'll save today.
tasks.expect: A list of three to five requests, each written as something you do, starting with a verb. If any line is a topic instead of a task (you wrote "marketing" instead of "write the newsletter email"), rewrite it.
tasks.stuck: If nothing comes to mind, open your chat history and look at the titles of your last fifteen conversations. The topics that repeat in those titles are exactly your list.

tasks.title: Rescue your best prompt from history
tasks.where: In the ChatGPT app or website (or Claude's, if that's where you work)
tasks.action: At the top of the left panel there's a magnifying glass or a box that says "Search chats." Click it and type a word you're sure you typed in that good conversation: a product name, a customer's name, an unusual word from your field. Open the results, find your LONGEST message (not the AI's) and copy it in full. Pay special attention to messages you wrote after correcting the AI ("no, shorter," "no exclamation points"): those corrections are the valuable part and need to go inside the prompt.
tasks.expect: You've copied a message of yours at least four or five lines long, plus the corrections you made afterward.
tasks.stuck: If you can't find anything usable, don't spend more than five minutes on it: write the request from scratch right now in the text box, with all the detail you can think of, and use that text instead. It works just as well for the next task.

tasks.title: Turn that request into a template with blanks
tasks.where: In the ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini text box
tasks.action: Open a new conversation and paste the prompt below. Where you see brackets, put in the message you rescued in the previous task and the corrections you made to it. When it gives you the template, read it and manually remove anything that isn't true: the AI sometimes adds conditions you never asked for.
tasks.prompt:
You're an expert at writing instructions for AI. I'm going to paste a message I wrote to an AI that worked well. I want to turn it into a template I can reuse every week without rethinking it.

The message that worked was this:
[PASTE YOUR MESSAGE HERE, TYPOS AND ALL]

And here are the corrections I made afterward:
[PASTE WHAT YOU TOLD IT TO FIX. IF YOU DIDN'T CORRECT ANYTHING, WRITE: none]

Do three things, in this order:
1) Tell me in four lines which parts of my message made the answer come out well, and which parts are extra.
2) Rewrite it as a reusable template. Everything that changes each time becomes a blank, in CAPITAL LETTERS and brackets, with a name that's self-explanatory: [PRODUCT NAME], never [X]. Everything that's always the same stays written in fixed. Fold in the corrections I pasted above, so I never have to make them again. Add at the end, if it's not there already, the exact response format and a word limit.
3) Below that, give me the list of blanks and, next to each, a real example of what to fill it with.

Don't give me three versions or ask me questions: give me one template and make it the right one. Five blanks maximum; if you get more, merge several into one. Direct, no fluff.
tasks.expect: A block of text with fixed parts and two to five capitalized blanks, with the blank list and examples below it. Read it in full: you should be able to fill it in without thinking.
tasks.stuck: If it gives you back a template full of blanks like [CONTEXT] or [GOAL], reply: "The blanks need to be concrete data I have on hand, not concepts. Rewrite it with four blanks maximum, each one a piece of data I could copy off a piece of paper."

tasks.title: Create the Prompt Library file
tasks.where: In a Google Doc, phone Notes, or a desktop Word file. Just one
tasks.action: Create a new document and call it "Prompt Library." Save it somewhere you'll find without searching: your desktop or your Drive's main folder. Now go back to the AI, paste the prompt below with the template you just got, and copy the entry it gives you into the document. Repeat with the other requests on your list until you have three or four entries.
tasks.prompt:
I want to build my prompt library in a single document and need every entry to have exactly the same shape. I'll give you a template and you convert it into an entry.

Template:
[PASTE THE TEMPLATE YOU JUST GOT HERE]

Give it back to me with this exact structure, no extra sections or comments from you:

NAME: a title starting with a verb, fitting in five words.
WHEN I USE IT: one sentence with the specific time of day or week I need it.
BLANKS: the list of what I need to fill in before sending it, with a real example next to each.
PROMPT: the complete text, ready to copy, no surrounding quotes, no bold.
HOW I KNOW IT WORKED: two or three concrete signals checkable at a glance. Nothing like "is clear"; things like "has fewer than 90 words" or "the word experience doesn't appear."
VERSION: v1 and today's date.

Plain text, no tables, so I can paste it anywhere.
tasks.expect: A document with at least three entries, all with the same six sections in the same order. It should fit in two pages.
tasks.stuck: If the document feels overwhelming, start with a phone note with a single entry. A one-prompt library already saves you time; a perfect library that doesn't exist doesn't.

tasks.title: Create your first Project in ChatGPT
tasks.where: In the ChatGPT app or website (chatgpt.com)
tasks.action: Look at the left panel, where your conversation list is. Above that list there's a section that says "Projects" with a + next to it; on mobile you may need to open that panel by swiping from the left edge. Click the +, name the project, and create it. The name is for you, so be literal: "Climbing shop listings" or "My practice's website," never "Work." Once it opens you'll see the conversation box in the middle and, at the top or in a side panel, two things: "Instructions" and "Files" (or "Add files").
tasks.expect: A project created, its name visible at the top, and an empty area to add instructions and files. You haven't written anything inside yet.
tasks.stuck: If you don't see "Projects" in the panel, update the app from your app store or go through the browser to chatgpt.com, where the newest version always lives. If it still doesn't show up, build the same thing with a starter prompt you paste at the beginning of every conversation: you lose convenience, not the result.

tasks.title: Write the project's instructions
tasks.action: Before writing them by hand, have them drafted for you. Open a regular conversation, outside the project, paste the prompt below, and fill in the brackets with the truth of your case. When it gives you back the text, read it line by line and delete any sentence that isn't a concrete order. Then copy the result and paste it into the project's "Instructions" box. On many screens there's no save button: it saves automatically when you leave the box, so close and reopen it to confirm the text is still there.
tasks.prompt:
You're going to write the instructions for an AI project. This isn't a message for a single conversation: it's the text that stays saved and that the AI will read at the start of every conversation in this project, forever.

This project is about: [DESCRIBE IN THREE SENTENCES WHAT WORK YOU DO HERE. EXAMPLE: I write the product listings and emails for a climbing gear shop in Vitoria; my customers are mountaineers 25 to 50; I have 300 products in the catalog].
What I always want: [EXAMPLE: plain casual English, short sentences, 90 words max].
What I never want: [EXAMPLE: emojis, exclamation points, the word experience, and never making up measurements, weights, or prices].
How I work: [EXAMPLE: I give you four loose facts and want the whole listing at once, no questions asked first].

Write me those instructions in under 250 words, addressing the AI directly ("you are," "write," "don't use"). Order them like this: who you are, what we do here, how you write, what you never do, and what you do when you're missing a fact. Every line needs to be an order that can be followed or broken; no pretty phrases like "be useful" or "be professional," which mean nothing. At the end, outside that text, tell me in two lines what you've assumed about me.
tasks.expect: A text under 250 words inside the instructions box, written as orders. If rereading it you find a sentence you can't tell whether it's being followed or not, delete it.
tasks.stuck: If you get brochure text full of "excellence" and "quality," reply: "Rewrite it with half the words and make every line a verifiable order. Remove any adjective that can't be measured."

tasks.title: Upload the files the AI should always know
tasks.where: In your project's "Files" or "Add files" section
tasks.action: Upload two to four files, not twenty. The three that pay off the most: one with your real data (price list, catalog, hours, terms), one with your tone (three or four old texts of yours you like, copied into a single document), and one with your rules (what to never say, how your product names are written, your real turnaround times). PDF, Word, Excel, and plain text all work. Before uploading anything, open each file and check it doesn't carry customer personal data: names, phone numbers, account numbers, addresses. If it does, remove it from the file before uploading.
tasks.expect: Two to four files listed in the project, each with its name. If it warns you you've hit your plan's limit, delete the least useful one.
tasks.stuck: If you don't have any document ready, create one in five minutes: copy and paste into a blank document three texts of yours that represent you (an email, an ad, a description) and upload it named "How I write."

tasks.title: Test the project cold
tasks.where: Inside the project, in a new conversation
tasks.action: Open a new conversation INSIDE the project: the button is on the project's own screen, not the general panel. Ask for the most typical request with no context at all. That's the whole point: if you have to explain who you are again, the instructions aren't doing their job. Paste the prompt below.
tasks.prompt:
With no extra context from me: write me [THE MOST TYPICAL REQUEST FOR THIS PROJECT. EXAMPLE: the listing for the Petzl Corax product, a $65 climbing harness].

Before starting, tell me in a single line which instructions you're following and which project files you looked at. Then, the actual request. And at the end, in two lines, tell me what fact you were missing and where you got it from.
tasks.expect: An answer that already comes with your tone, format, and length without you asking for any of that, plus a line at the start acknowledging your instructions and files.
tasks.stuck: If it ignores the instructions, it's almost always one of two things: the text never actually saved (go back to the instructions box and check it's still there) or you opened the conversation outside the project. Check the top: the project's name has to appear in the conversation.

tasks.title: Set up the same thing in Claude without paying anything
tasks.where: In the Claude app or website (claude.ai)
tasks.action: Click your initial or photo at the bottom left, go into "Settings," and look inside your profile for the box asking what personal preferences Claude should keep in mind. That box is free and applies to all your conversations. Generate the text with the prompt below, paste it there, and save. Then, next to any conversation's text box, look for the "Style" button and create your own by pasting in three texts of yours: that fixes how it sounds, no money spent. If "Projects" also shows up because you have a paid plan, create one and paste in the same instructions you wrote for ChatGPT: they work the same way.
tasks.prompt:
Write me the text for my personal preferences in Claude: what I want it to keep in mind across all my conversations, whatever the topic.

Who I am and what I do: [TWO SENTENCES].
How I want it to talk to me: [EXAMPLE: plain casual English, direct, don't recap what I just said before answering].
What bugs me: [EXAMPLE: starting with "Great question!", giving me three options when I asked for one, turning everything into a list, apologizing].
My technical level: I've never coded; if you use a technical word, translate it in parentheses the first time it appears.

Maximum 150 words, second person, only orders that can be followed or broken. Nothing like "be useful" or "be clear," which mean nothing. Give me the plain text, ready to paste into a settings box, no headers or bullet points.
tasks.expect: The text saved in your Claude settings, and a new conversation where it already answers in that tone without you asking. Test it with any random question.
tasks.stuck: If you can't find the box, check Settings inside your profile or personalization section; the names change every few months. If it's still not there, paste your preferences at the start of the conversation instead: it costs five seconds and does the same job.

tasks.title: Add version and date, and schedule your review
tasks.action: Go back to the document and, on the entry you just actually used, update the version field: if you had to correct the AI during the test, fold that correction into the prompt and bump it to v2 with today's date. Write a line at the very top of the document that says "Review all of this on [date three months out]." And add a rule for yourself: when a prompt fails you twice in a row, don't patch it in the chat, fix it here.
tasks.expect: At least one entry on v2 with its date, and a review-reminder line at the top of the document.
tasks.stuck: If versioning feels like too much, keep the bare minimum: the date. Knowing a prompt hasn't been touched in eight months already tells you plenty.

matters: Putting each instruction in the right drawer. What you write in global instructions affects everything, including conversations that have nothing to do with it: put "answer in under 100 words" there and the AI will cut off the three-page email you need for a client, and it'll take you weeks to figure out why.

Writing, in every prompt, how you'll know it turned out well. Without those two checkable signals you end up reading whole answers and deciding by feel, which is exactly what makes you accept text that sounds great and has a made-up fact buried in it.

Uploading your real data to the project as a file. An AI without your prices, measurements, and turnaround times in front of it fills those gaps with reasonable-sounding, false numbers, and those are the ones that end up published on your site or sent to a customer.

Keeping the library in one single place. The moment you scatter it across phone notes, a Word file, and three saved conversations, you stop using it within a month and go back to writing everything from memory, which is exactly the problem you were trying to escape.
ignore: Paid prompt-management tools (managers, browser extensions, apps with folders and tags). They cost $8 to $20 a month and solve a problem you don't have yet: with seven prompts, a document is faster.

Serious version control, with Git and repositories. That's the professional way to track changes and it'll come eventually; today writing "v2 - 03/12/2026" next to the prompt does the same job without making you open a terminal.
Setting up a project for every single thing you do. Two well-used projects are worth more than eleven empty ones, and the empty ones clutter the panel until you stop looking at it.
canDo: Turn a messy message of yours into a clean template with blanks, and tell you along the way which part was the one making the answer come out well.
Draft a project's instructions in 200 words from four sentences of yours, and warn you at the end about what it assumed about you.
Read the files you upload to the project and use your prices, measurements, and old texts instead of making up its own.
Copy your writing style with decent accuracy if you give it three or four real texts of yours, far better than if you describe it with adjectives.
cantDo: It can't go into your old conversations to dig up that prompt that worked for you. Every conversation starts blind: the rescue is on you, using the history search.
It doesn't warn you you've been repeating the same request for six weeks. Nobody's going to tell you "you've already asked this four times, save it"; that warning is on you.
It doesn't sync anything between ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini. What you save in a ChatGPT project doesn't exist for Claude, and vice versa: that's why your prompt file lives outside all three.
It doesn't recover a deleted project or the conversations that were inside it. That button has no recycle bin, so copy important prompts to your document before deleting anything.
words: Prompt
The message you write to the AI in the text box. Everything you ask for, with its context and conditions, is the prompt.
Template
A prompt written once and left deliberately half-filled: the part that doesn't change stays written, and whatever changes each time gets marked with brackets so you fill it in on the spot.
Blank
That piece you leave marked in brackets and capital letters inside a template, like [PRICE IN DOLLARS]. It's the only thing you touch before sending the message.
Project

A folder inside ChatGPT or Claude where you put instructions and files. Everything you say inside that folder arrives already carrying those instructions and files, without you pasting them each time.
Project instructions
The text saved inside a project that says who the AI is in there, how it writes, and what it never does. It reads it at the start of every conversation in that project, and you never write it again.
Custom instructions

The same thing, but for your whole account: it affects any conversation you have with that AI, on any topic. In ChatGPT they're under Settings, inside Personalization; in Claude, under Settings, inside your profile.
Memory
A feature that automatically picks up loose bits from your conversations to remember later. You don't control it, so it's not a place to save prompts.
Style
A Claude feature that fixes how the answer sounds (how long, the tone, the rhythm) without changing what it says. You can build your own by pasting in texts you wrote.
Knowledge base
The files you upload to a project so the AI always has them in front of it: your catalog, your prices, your old texts. In Claude it appears as "project knowledge."
Version
The number you give a prompt every time you improve it (v1, v2, v3) with the date next to it. It tells you whether a prompt is fresh or hasn't been touched in eight months.
next: Take the second request from your list, turn it into a template with the same prompt from task three, and save it in the document: with five entries in it, the library starts giving you back hours every week.
